analysis.summary: Kubernetes v1.37.0-beta.0 是一个功能丰富的版本，重点关注调度增强（PodGroup、Workload-Aware Preemption）、DRA（Dynamic Resource Allocation）稳定性和关键 Bug 修复，包含多项 API 升级和重要的安全修复。
key_changes: metrics.k8s.io API 从 v1beta1 升级到 GA (v1) - [PR #139223](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139223)
ClusterTrustBundles 功能升级到 GA 并默认启用 - [PR #139437](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139437)
为 StatefulSet 新增 Recreate 更新策略 - [PR #137187](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137187)
引入 Node 生命周期条件（GracefulNodeShutdownInProgress, DrainInProgress 等） - [PR #139993](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139993)
PodGroup 核心 API 实现（KEP-6012） - [PR #139596](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139596)
为 PodGroup 调度新增 PodGroupPostFilter 扩展点 - [PR #139674](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139674)
支持原地 Pod 垂直扩缩容的调度器抢占（Alpha 特性） - [PR #140000](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140000)
EtcdRangeStream 特性门默认启用（Beta），提升 watch-cache 初始化性能 - [PR #140085](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140085)
NativeHistograms 特性门升级到 Beta - [PR #140124](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140124)
important_bugfixes: 修复 kube-apiserver 在身份 Lease 无法创建时（如主机名超过 63 字节）收到 SIGTERM 后死锁无法关闭的问题 - [PR #140241](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140241) - **影响：** 导致 apiserver 无法正常关闭，只能通过 SIGKILL 强制终止，影响集群维护和滚动升级
修复 kube-proxy 在节点 IP 变更或节点删除后不重启，导致网络状态过时的问题 - [PR #138183](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138183) - **影响：** 节点网络配置变更后 kube-proxy 可能使用旧的网络信息，导致服务流量路由错误
修复 DRA 结构化分配器在拒绝或回溯候选设备时泄漏预留计数器和约束的问题 - [PR #140431](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140431) - **影响：** 可能导致可调度的 Pod 因资源计数错误而持续处于 Pending 状态
修复 CEL 准入控制器在处理三键类型 Map 列表时可能 panic 的问题 - [PR #140386](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140386) - **影响：** 特定 CEL 验证规则可能导致 apiserver 崩溃
修复 Burstable QoS Pod 的 memory.low cgroup 设置因缺少祖先覆盖而无效的问题 - [PR #140267](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140267) - **影响：** Burstable Pod 的内存保护可能不生效，在内存压力下被过早驱逐
修复 kubelet 在跨资源设备 ID 冲突时将设备健康更新路由到错误 Pod 的问题 - [PR #140323](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140323) - **影响：** 设备健康状态更新可能影响错误的 Pod，导致不必要的状态同步和潜在调度问题
修复 DRA ResourceSlice 控制器在快速删除后更新时使用 MutationCache 中过时副本的问题 - [PR #140063](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140063) - **影响：** DRA 驱动重启更新期间，kubelet 删除 ResourceSlice 后控制器可能无法正确重新创建
修复容器状态中 Linux UID 大于 INT32_MAX 时被错误拒绝的问题 - [PR #138574](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138574) - **影响：** 使用高 UID（> 2,147,483,647）的容器会卡在 ContainerCreating 状态
修复启用 DRAListTypeAttributes 时，matchAttribute 约束在回溯期间交集计算错误导致设备分配失败的问题 - [PR #140325](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140325) - **影响：** 存在有效设备组合时调度失败
修复 CEL 对 'set' 和 'map' 列表的相等性和连接操作语义 - [PR #140293](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140293) - **影响：** CEL 验证规则中涉及列表相等和连接的操作可能产生意外结果
security_issues: 修复 kubectl cluster-info dump 输出文件权限过宽，可能泄露 Pod 日志中敏感信息的问题 - [PR #140189](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140189) - **风险级别：** 高 - 之前文件默认创建为 0644（全局可读），Pod 日志常包含令牌、凭证等敏感信息
更新 kube-proxy 镜像中的 nftables 到 1.0.6.1，修复与系统上较新 nftables 版本不兼容导致的崩溃 - [PR #140405](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140405) - **风险级别：** 中 - 可能导致 kube-proxy 持续崩溃，影响集群网络
performance_improvements: 在 kube-proxy informer 中剥离 managedFields 以减少缓存大小 - [PR #140056](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140056) - **提升：** 显著减少 kube-proxy 内存使用，特别是大型集群
默认启用 EtcdRangeStream 特性门，优化 watch-cache 初始化 - [PR #140085](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140085) - **提升：** watch-cache 初始化速度提升约 30%，内存使用减少约 9%
调度器指标 plugin_execution_duration_seconds 和 scheduling_algorithm_duration_seconds 升级到 BETA - [PR #138176](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138176) - **提升：** 提供更稳定的调度性能监控指标
新增 PodGroup 级别调度队列指标 - [PR #139840](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139840) - **提升：** 增强对 Gang Scheduling 工作负载的监控能力
breaking_changes: CEL 表达式对 'set' 和 'map' 类型列表的相等性（==）和连接（+）操作语义变更 - [PR #140293](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140293) - **影响：** 需要检查并更新所有使用 CEL 进行列表比较或连接的验证规则，确保新语义下仍能正确工作
MutatingAdmissionPolicy 存储版本覆盖在 v1.37 中移除 - [Issue #138283](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138283) - **影响：** 使用 MutatingAdmissionPolicy 的用户需确保客户端兼容 v1 API 版本
kubectl cluster-info dump 输出文件权限从 0644 改为 0600，目录权限从 0755 改为 0700 - [PR #140189](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140189) - **影响：** 自动化脚本若依赖其他用户读取 dump 输出需调整，或修改脚本以适当权限运行
kube-proxy --metrics-bind-address 文档修正：空字符串不再禁用指标服务器，而是回退到默认地址 - [PR #138940](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138940) - **影响：** 依赖文档中“设为空以禁用”行为的用户需改用其他方法禁用指标服务器
recommendations: **立即行动：** 如果使用 kubectl cluster-info dump 进行故障排查，升级到该版本以修复敏感信息泄露漏洞。检查现有 dump 文件权限并清理。
**测试重点：** 升级前在测试环境中充分验证 CEL 准入策略，特别是涉及列表操作的部分。
**DRA 用户：** 如果使用 Dynamic Resource Allocation 和设备插件，仔细测试设备分配和健康监控功能，确保修复生效。
**调度优化：** 关注 PodGroup 和 Workload-Aware Preemption 相关功能，评估其对批处理工作负载调度的影响。
**监控更新：** 利用新的调度器 BETA 指标和 PodGroup 级别指标优化监控和告警。
**升级准备：** 确保主机名不超过 63 字节，避免触发 kube-apiserver 关闭死锁问题（虽已修复，但仍建议规范命名）。
**权限检查：** 审查所有依赖 kubectl cluster-info dump 输出的自动化流程，确保有适当权限读取新创建的文件。
analysis.risk_assessment: 整体风险评估：中等。此版本包含多个关键稳定性修复和安全补丁，建议升级。主要风险来自 CEL 语义变更可能破坏现有验证规则，以及 DRA 相关改动可能影响设备感知调度。建议的升级时机：在充分测试 CEL 策略和 DRA 功能后，尽快安排升级以获取安全修复。需要特别关注的方面：1) CEL 验证规则测试；2) DRA 设备分配功能验证；3) 调度器行为变化对工作负载的影响；4) kubectl 权限变更对自动化流程的影响。

134037.title: KEP-3926: implement dry-run support for unsafe corrupt object deletion
134037.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This PR implements dry-run support for the unsafe corrupt object deletion feature introduced in KEP-3926.

This enhancement allows administrators to safely test corrupt object deletion operations before executing them, providing an important safety mechanism for this potentially cluster-breaking operation.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
 
Fixes #

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

This builds upon the existing unsafe deletion functionality from #127513. The dry-run implementation follows Kubernetes' standard dry-run patterns and maintains backward compatibility.

Key changes:

- Removed validation restriction in that blocked dry-run with unsafe deletion options
- Enhanced `corrupt_obj_deleter.go` to handle dry-run requests appropriately
- Added comprehensive test coverage for dry-run scenarios in integration tests

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

This feature is feature-gated by `AllowUnsafeMalformedObjectDeletion`:

```release-note
The unsafe corrupt object deletion feature now supports dry-run mode, allowing administrators to test deletion operations safely before execution.
```

#### Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.:

- KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/3927

138574.title: pkg/apis/core: allow uint32 Linux UIDs in container status
138574.body:
## What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig node

## What this PR does / why we need it

Linux UIDs are unsigned 32-bit values, but pod status validation currently uses the existing Kubernetes pod spec UID validator, which is limited to `math.MaxInt32`. When a runtime reports `containerStatus.user.linux.uid` above `2147483647`, kubelet status updates can be rejected even though the reported UID is valid on Linux.

This PR keeps pod spec `runAsUser` and kubelet image user validation on the existing int32 UID range, and only accepts the full unsigned 32-bit Linux UID range for reported container user fields in pod status. GID and supplemental group validation remain unchanged.

140063.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When updating a ResourceSlice, a more recent copy than in the underlying store gets cached by the MutationCache. Then when that ResourceSlice gets deleted on the apiserver and then the store, the MutationCache kept the stale copy and returned it when the controller synced again, causing the controller to erroneously not recreate the deleted ResourceSlice.

Depending on timing, this could have happened while updating the DRA driver:
- Driver restarts, updating the existing ResourceSlices.
- kubelet deletes the slices before realizing that the driver is running again.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

N/A

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

The fix is to address a long-standing TODO in the MutationCache: it needs to react to changes in the store. This allows it to drop cached objects sooner and let's it remove cached objects that are known to be deleted. Users of a MutationCache must inform the cache in their own informer event handlers *before* triggering sync operations.

This is a different approach than the one taken in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140011 where the staleness was detected via a timed resync. Such a timed resync is still needed after adding a ResourceSlice.

This includes your integration test. The test also passed for me with current master, but that might have been just luck. We need a test which triggers the bug more reliably and of course also unit tests.

This needs changes in client-go tooling.

140189.title: kubectl: create cluster-info dump output with owner-only permissions
140189.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig cli
/sig security
/area kubectl

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`kubectl cluster-info dump --output-directory` writes every dump file through `setupOutputWriter`, which used `os.Create` (mode `0666` before umask, typically `0644`) inside directories created with `os.MkdirAll(parent, 0755)`. Pod logs are dumped verbatim into `{dir}/{namespace}/{pod}/logs.txt`, and pod logs routinely contain application secrets (bearer tokens, connection strings, cloud credentials). With `--all-namespaces` this includes logs from namespaces the local reader would have no RBAC right to see. Any unprivileged local user on the machine where the operator ran the dump could read all of it.

This PR creates dump files with mode `0600` and kubectl-created directories with `0700`, so cluster state dumped to disk is readable only by the user who ran the command.

140241.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/kind regression
/sig api-machinery

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Since 1.35, kube-apiserver deadlocks on SIGTERM when its identity Lease can never
be created (for example, a hostname longer than the 63-byte label limit). The
lease controller's `sync()` holds `reconcilingLock` while retrying the create
forever, and the pre-shutdown hook calls `Stop()`, which blocks on that lock. The
context that would end the retries is only canceled after the pre-shutdown hooks
return, so shutdown never begins and only SIGKILL ends the process.

retry wait in `backoffEnsureLease` return when it fires. `Stop()` now returns
promptly and shutdown proceeds; the lease errors still log, but no longer block
anything.

It also adds a regression test. Without the `controller.go` change, the test hangs
in the same 7-second retry loop and fails after 30 seconds; with it, it passes in
milliseconds.

Verified with real binaries: on a host with a 64-byte hostname, the official
v1.35.0 and v1.36.2 apiservers ignore SIGTERM indefinitely, while a build with
this fix exits about 2 seconds after SIGTERM. Full analysis, goroutine dump, and
reproducers are in the linked issue.

Introduced by #134514 (v1.35.0).

140323.title: kubelet: fix device health updates being routed to the wrong pod when device IDs collide across resources
140323.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/kind flake
/sig node
/wg device-management

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When a device plugin reports a health change, the device manager looks up which pod owns the affected device so it can trigger a status sync for that pod. The lookup in [`getPodAndContainerForDevice`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dd3e7940568f7156dabf8b3f13295e6a6469b4c8/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/pod_devices.go#L184-L198) matched on the device ID alone, iterating over all pods and all resources. Device IDs are only unique within a single resource, so when two plugins expose devices with the same ID under different resource names, the lookup can return a pod that owns the same device ID under an unrelated resource, and Go map iteration order makes the result nondeterministic.

When that happens, [`genericDeviceUpdateCallback`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dd3e7940568f7156dabf8b3f13295e6a6469b4c8/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L293-L346) sends the update notification for the wrong pod, the [syncLoop handler](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dd3e7940568f7156dabf8b3f13295e6a6469b4c8/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2817-L2832) syncs that wrong pod, and the pod that actually owns the unhealthy device does not get its `allocatedResourcesStatus` updated until the next periodic sync, up to a minute later.

This is the root cause of the flaking test tracked in #140268. Every spec in [`device_plugin_failures_pod_status_test.go`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dd3e7940568f7156dabf8b3f13295e6a6469b4c8/test/e2e_node/device_plugin_failures_pod_status_test.go#L131) registers its device as `testdevice` under a randomized resource name. When two of those specs run close together on the same node, which happens regularly in the parallel CI jobs, the health update from one spec is delivered to the other spec's pod and the 60 second `Eventually` in the test loses the race against the periodic sync. The kubelet log of failing run `ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd/2074205743732494336` shows exactly this: the device for resource `test.device/device-plugin-failures-3083` goes unhealthy while the forwarded sync event carries the pod UID of the previous spec's pod from namespace `device-plugin-failures-5477`, and the right pod only flipped to Unhealthy at the next periodic sync, 2.4 seconds after the test timeout.

The fix scopes the lookup by resource name, which the callback already has on hand.

I reproduced the flake by running the two `Device Plugin Failures Pod Status` specs concurrently against a stock kubelet on a GCE Ubuntu 24.04 VM with containerd (`ginkgo -nodes=2 -focus="Device Plugin Failures Pod Status" e2e_node.test`, mirroring how the CI jobs share one kubelet across parallel ginkgo processes). It failed on the first iteration with the exact CI signature. With the fixed kubelet the same loop ran 10 consecutive iterations with zero failures, and every health transition in the kubelet log was routed to the pod in the matching namespace. `TestGetPodAndContainerForDevice` now also covers the collision case: the same device ID allocated to two pods under different resource names resolves to the correct pod for each resource.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

Fixes #140268

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
kubelet: fixed device health updates being applied to the wrong pod's status when device plugins for different resources expose devices with identical IDs. Affected pods now reflect device health changes immediately instead of waiting for the next periodic pod sync.
```

140431.title: DRA: roll back reserved state in allocateDevice
140431.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig node

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The structured DRA allocator can leave reserved state behind when it stops considering a candidate device, which can make a schedulable pod fail to schedule.

allocateDevice reserves a device's shared counters and adds claim constraints before it may reject a candidate on a device taint or a claim constraint. For a candidate it accepts, it also marks the device in use and reserves consumable capacity, and the backtracking search later has to undo all of that. Some of these paths did not reverse what they had done. The taint and constraint rejections left the reserved counters in place, and the success undo for an allow-multiple device released its capacity but not the counters it had reserved on its first allocation. A leaked counter reservation makes the allocator treat a counter set as exhausted, so it fails to allocate a device combination a node can satisfy.

Each call now records what it mutated in a small `deviceRollbackState` value and reverses it with one `rollbackDevice` method. Every rejection path after a successful counter reservation calls it, including the must error path, and the success path returns a closure that calls the same method, so the rejection cleanup and the backtracking undo can no longer drift apart. The capacity check runs before the capacity reservation, so a capacity rejection does not leak capacity. What it can leave behind is the claim constraint added just before the check, which `rollbackDevice` now removes.

The same rollback exposed a second miscount for allow-multiple devices that consume counters but have no consumable capacity. allocateDevice still inserts an empty entry into the capacity map for such a device, and that entry doubles as the marker that lets a later share of the device skip the counter check. The capacity collection does not reference-count empty entries, so when several shares of the device exist in one search and the rollback removes one, it deletes the marker while another share is still active, and a later share is then wrongly rejected with insufficient counters. The rollback now records whether the entry predated the share it is undoing and restores an empty marker when removing it would drop one that a surviving share still relies on.

The state is passed by value so the rejection paths keep it on the stack, and only the success path allocates a closure. allocateDevice runs in the scheduler's per-node exhaustive search where the common outcome is rejection, so this avoids adding a heap allocation for the rollback bookkeeping on rejected candidates. Building the undo closure up front and returning it would move the closure and its captured flags to the heap on every rejected candidate; `go build -gcflags=-m` confirms that with this change only the success path builds the escaping undo closure.

All three allocator variants (stable, incubating, experimental) share the same shape and are fixed together. This matters because the default feature configuration selects incubating, not stable: ConsumableCapacity and the device binding and status features are on by default and stable does not support them, so `NewAllocator` picks incubating. The bug was reachable on default clusters, not only the non-default stable variant.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #140436

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

The regression cases live in the shared `allocatortesting` table so they run against every variant that supports the required features, and they assert the exact allocated devices:

- `partitionable-devices-taint-releases-counter` and `partitionable-devices-constraint-releases-counter` cover the counter leak on the taint and constraint rejection paths.
- `partitionable-consumable-capacity-backtrack-releases-counter` covers the allow-multiple device that reserved a counter on its first allocation and must release it when the search backtracks.
- `consumable-capacity-rejection-rolls-back-constraints` covers the claim constraint left behind when an all-mode candidate is rejected on the in-function capacity check.
- `partitionable-empty-capacity-multiple-share-backtrack-keeps-counter-ownership` covers the empty-capacity device whose shared marker must survive a sibling share's backtracking.
- `partitionable-all-mode-constraint-must-error-with-reserved-counter` covers the must error path when the rejected device has reserved a counter.

`go test ./structured/...` is green with the change, including `-race`. The taint, constraint, backtrack, and capacity-rejection cases fail without the fix. The empty-capacity marker case fails if the rollback removes a shared marker a sibling share still holds. The must error case adds coverage of that path; the error aborts the allocation, so the rollback runs there but its effect is not separately observable.

Concurrent work: independent of #140435 (counter cache pool identity). #140437 (skip counter check for a persisted shared device) is related but separable: it and the shared-marker fix here address the same shared-device counter accounting from two sides, persisted shares across scheduling cycles there and in-flight shares within one search here. They still compose; the allocator source merges cleanly and only the shared `allocatortesting` table needs a trivial rebase for whichever lands second. #140084 and #139795 add counter and compatibility state to the same `allocateDevice` path; when they rebase, that state should be recorded in `deviceRollbackState` and undone by `rollbackDevice` rather than through a separate cleanup path.

/cc @pohly @klueska

```release-note
Fixed DRA scheduling bugs where the structured allocator mis-counted a device's shared counters while exploring candidates: it could keep a counter reserved after rejecting or backtracking a candidate, or drop a shared device's in-use marker so a later share was charged the counter twice. Either way the allocator could treat a counter set as exhausted and leave a pod pending on a node that could satisfy it. This affected the allocator used by the default feature configuration.
```

137981.title: Feature/pod group as victim
137981.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
This PR enhances the standard Pod-by-Pod preemption flow to support PodGroups as preemption victims. Previously, the preemption logic treated all pods individually. With this change, if a pod belongs to a PodGroup, the preemption logic can treat the group as a single atomic victim.

High-level overview of how this was achieved:
- **Interface Abstraction**: Introduced `Victim` and `DomainVictim` separation.
    - **`Victim`**: A general type used to generalize single Pods and `PodGroups`. It supports operations that do not depend on a specific preemption domain.
    - **`DomainVictim`**: Tied strictly to a preemption domain. It tracks `nodeInfos` (copies of node state, not active snapshot references, except WAP flow, for WAP we are using actual reference) representing the affected blast radius, which the preemption algorithm uses to identify pods for eviction. It cannot be created outside of a domain.
- **Constructor Methods**:

138809.title: kubectl explain: add --max-depth flag
138809.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

`/kind feature
`

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`kubectl explain --recursive` prints the full schema tree for a resource. For large resources (Pod, Deployment, CRDs with deeply nested specs), the output is hundreds of lines and there is no way to ask for a shallower overview short of navigating field-by-field with dotted paths.

This PR adds a new `--max-depth=N` flag to `kubectl explain` that caps recursion depth when printing nested fields:
- `--max-depth=0` (default) preserves the existing unlimited behavior.
- `--max-depth=N` (N > 0) prints fields up to N levels and implies `--recursive`.
- Negative values are rejected at validation time.

The cap is threaded through both render paths so behavior is consistent regardless of which one runs:
- v1 (OpenAPIv2): `recursiveFieldsPrinter` carries a depth counter and skips child recursion at the limit.
- v2 (OpenAPIv3, default): the plaintext template guards `fieldList` recursion on `lt $.level $.MaxDepth`.

When recursion stops at the limit, the field name and type marker (e.g., `spec\t<PodSpec>`) are still printed, so users see what exists and can drill down with a field path or a deeper `--max-depth`.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Fixes kubernetes/kubectl#1659

#### Special notes:

The flag is purely additive and backward compatible: the default `MaxDepth=0` is treated as unlimited, so existing `--recursive` invocations are unchanged. Tests cover validation, the v1 printer, the v2 template, and the CLI wiring; `test/cmd/discovery.sh` also exercises the flag end-to-end against a CRD.

Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Added a `--max-depth` flag to `kubectl explain --recursive` to limit the depth of nested fields displayed in the output.
```

139980.title: Reimplement WAP with in place filter reprieval
139980.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature


#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This PR aligns the implementation of the Workload-Aware Preemption with the description of it from the KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-scheduling/5710-workload-aware-preemption/README.md

The main changes include:
- running only one scheduling algorithm after victims are removed
- reusing CycleStates from scheduling algorithm for victim reprieval
- running Filter plugins on each of the preemptors for victim reprieval

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5710

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

There is one little problem with this approach. Removing pods from NodeInfo in preemption does not change the state of `havePodsWithRequiredAntiAffinityNodeInfoList`, `havePodsWithAffinityNodeInfoList`, `usedPVCSet` in the Snapshot structure. The same issue currently exists in the pod group cycle and there is an open PR to resolve that:  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139054

However the lack of this support is not a blocker here as for all three fields in WAP we will produce false positives. For `havePodsWithRequiredAntiAffinityNodeInfoList` and `havePodsWithAffinityNodeInfoList` it means that we will potentially scan more nodes than necessary.  For usedPVCSet it means that we will not support a case where removing a pod with PVC would unblock scheduling of preemptor. This is on par with the current pod by pod preemption .

With this change the time needed to complete test scenarios from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139773 from minutes to seconds.  

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Workload-Aware Preemption now runs only one scheduling attempt, on a cluster with all potential victims removed. This can lead to a suboptimal preemption victims choice at the cost of significant performance improvement.
```

139996.title: Skip CriticalPodAdmissionHandler for resizes
139996.body:
### Proposal

Skip the `CriticalPodAdmissionHandler` when evaluating resize feasibility, contingent on the `SchedulerPreemptionForPodResize` feature gate.

### Background

The `CriticalPodAdmissionHandler` forcefully evicts pods from the node to make room for system-critical priority pods. This admission handler acts as a backstop, incase there was a disconnect between scheduling and node admission (for example, a [scheduler race](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/126891) or pod bypassing the scheduler).

This admission handler was included by default when we implemented in-place pod resize, meaning that resized critical pods will forcefully evict lower priority pods to make room for the resize.

### Motivation

The `CriticalPodAdmissionHandler` uses custom Kubelet preemption logic that differs form the scheduler preemption logic and doesn't consider PodDispruptionBudgets (PDBs), pod PreemptionPolicy, nor workload-aware scheduling.

Now that we're adding support for scheduler-based preemption on resize, I think we should stop triggering the Kubelet-managed system-critical preemptions on resize (but keep it as a backstop for new-pod admission).

/sig node

140095.title: kubectl: `cluster-info dump --output-directory` writes pod logs (with embedded secrets) as world-readable
140095.body:
### What happened?

`kubectl cluster-info dump --output-directory=DUMP` writes every dump file via `setupOutputWriter`, which does:

```go
// staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/clusterinfo/clusterinfo_dump.go:126 (func setupOutputWriter)
file, err := os.Create(fullFile)
```

`os.Create` opens files `O_RDWR|O_CREATE|O_TRUNC` with mode `0666` before umask. With the very common `0022` umask that is `0644` (world-readable); with `0002` (common on shared systems / some distros) it is `0664` (group- and other-readable). Parents are created `0755` (`os.MkdirAll(parent, 0755)` at line 124), so the directory tree is traversable by "other".

Pod logs are dumped verbatim to `{DUMP}/{namespace}/{pod}/logs.txt` (line 295 → `writer.Write(data)` at line 287, raw bytes straight from the `log` API). Pod logs routinely contain application secrets: bearer tokens, DB connection strings, cloud credentials, signed URLs, signed certificate/key material, etc.

### What did you expect to happen?

Dump files should be created owner-only (`0600`), and the dump directory tree owner-only (`0700`) when it contains pod logs or other potentially sensitive cluster state, so that an unprivileged local user cannot read the operator's cluster dump.

Preconditions on the victim host: another local user can traverse the path to DUMP (the typical case — DUMP in a home dir, `/tmp`, a shared scratch dir, or a CI artifact dir whose parents are `0755`). The attacker needs **no Kubernetes API credentials at all** — only filesystem read on files kubectl itself just created.

1. Authorized/privileged operator runs kubectl once:
   ```bash
   kubectl cluster-info dump --output-directory=DUMP --all-namespaces
   ```
   kubectl creates DUMP and all nested dirs `0755`, and every `logs.txt` (and `nodes.txt`, `events.txt`, …) `0644`/`0664`, with full pod-log contents — across **all** namespaces requested.
2. A second unprivileged local user reads the logs directly:
   ```bash
   cat $DUMP/*/leaky/logs.txt        # 044-mode readable + traversable parents (0755) => readable by "other"
   ```
   No exploit primitive required — ordinary filesystem ACLs. `--all-namespaces` widens the blast radius to logs from every namespace, including ones the attacker has no RBAC right to read.
3. Extract whatever secret the logs leaked (token, password, cert+key), then use it against the cluster or upstream systems:
   ```bash
   kubectl --token=<LEAKED> ...        # if a bearer token was logged
   # or use a leaked DB connection string / cloud credential against the corresponding backend
   ```
   → access beyond the attacker's normal reach, often as a high-privilege workload identity.

Exposure is **durable**: the files persist at `0644`/`0664` on disk under DUMP until someone manually tightens permissions or deletes them, and re-running the dump re-creates them the same way. On a shared host captured by automation, the window can stay open indefinitely.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run this single self-contained snippet from the root of a Kubernetes checkout. It spins up a fake API server that returns one pod whose `log` endpoint serves a secret marker, then runs the real `kubectl cluster-info dump` and reports the resulting file mode + leak. It uses an already-built `kubectl` (`_output/local/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl` or `_output/bin/kubectl`).

```bash
set -e
KUBECTL="${KUBECTL:-_output/local/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl}"
[ -x "$KUBECTL" ] || KUBECTL=_output/bin/kubectl
[ -x "$KUBECTL" ] || { echo "build kubectl first: make kubectl"; exit 1; }

python3 - "$PWD/$KUBECTL" <<'PY'
import http.server, json, os, pathlib, socket, stat, subprocess, sys, tempfile, threading, urllib.parse
kubectl_bin = sys.argv[1]
secret = "TOKEN=cluster-log-secret-12345\n"
def list_obj(kind, items=None):
    return {"apiVersion": "v1", "kind": kind, "metadata": {"resourceVersion": "1"}, "items": items or []}
def apps_list(kind):
    return {"apiVersion": "apps/v1", "kind": kind, "metadata": {"resourceVersion": "1"}, "items": []}
pod = {"apiVersion": "v1", "kind": "Pod",
       "metadata": {"name": "leaky", "namespace": "default", "uid": "11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111"},
       "spec": {"containers": [{"name": "app", "image": "busybox"}]}, "status": {"phase": "Running"}}

class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def log_message(self, *a): return
    def send_json(self, obj):
        d = json.dumps(obj).encode()
        self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(d))); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(d)

        if p == "/api/v1": return self.send_json({"kind": "APIResourceList", "apiVersion": "v1", "groupVersion": "v1", "resources": []})
        if p == "/apis": return self.send_json({"kind": "APIGroupList", "apiVersion": "v1", "groups": [{"name": "apps", "versions": [{"groupVersion": "apps/v1", "version": "v1"}], "preferredVersion": {"groupVersion": "apps/v1", "version": "v1"}}]})
        if p == "/apis/apps/v1": return self.send_json({"kind": "APIResourceList", "apiVersion": "v1", "groupVersion": "apps/v1", "resources": []})
        if p == "/api/v1/nodes": return self.send_json(list_obj("NodeList"))
        if p == "/api/v1/namespaces/default/events": return self.send_json(list_obj("EventList"))
        if p == "/api/v1/namespaces/default/replicationcontrollers": return self.send_json(list_obj("ReplicationControllerList"))

    s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0)); port = s.getsockname()[1]

threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
out = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="cluster-info-dump-poc-"); os.chmod(out, 0o755)
try:
    cmd = [kubectl_bin, f"--server=http://127.0.0.1:{port}", "--kubeconfig=/dev/null",
           "cluster-info", "dump", "--namespaces=default", "--output-directory=" + out, "-o", "json"]
    r = subprocess.run(cmd, text=True, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE)
    if r.returncode != 0:
        print("ERROR: kubectl cluster-info dump failed", file=sys.stderr)
        print(r.stdout, file=sys.stderr); print(r.stderr, file=sys.stderr); sys.exit(r.returncode)
    lp = pathlib.Path(out) / "default" / "leaky" / "logs.txt"
    content = lp.read_text(); mode = stat.S_IMODE(lp.stat().st_mode)
    print(f"kubectl        : {kubectl_bin}")
    print(f"dump_dir       : {out}")
    print(f"log_file       : {lp}")

    print(f"contains_secret: {secret.strip() in content}")
    print(f"other_readable : {bool(mode & 0o004)}")
    if (mode & 0o004) and secret.strip() in content:

    srv.shutdown()
```

Expected output (observed; mode depends on umask — `0644` under `0022`, `0664` under `0002`, both other-readable):

```text
kubectl        : .../kubectl
dump_dir       : /tmp/cluster-info-dump-poc-XXXX
log_file       : /tmp/cluster-info-dump-poc-XXXX/default/leaky/logs.txt

```

The pod log containing the secret marker is written to a mode-`0664` (or `0644`) file readable by other local users. No API binding or real cluster is involved.

### Anything else we need to know?

- Sink: `staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/clusterinfo/clusterinfo_dump.go:126`, `func setupOutputWriter`, called from the dump path (e.g. pod logs at line 295; also nodes/events/services/pods/etc.). Parents created `0755` at line 124.

### What happened?

On hosts with hostnames longer than 63 bytes, `kube-apiserver` does not shut down after `SIGTERM`. It keeps serving until `SIGKILL`.

This reproduces consistently with official v1.35.0 and v1.36.2 binaries on Linux and macOS. v1.34 shuts down normally on the same hosts.

The hostname matters because the apiserver identity Lease is labeled with `kubernetes.io/hostname`, and Kubernetes label values are limited to 63 bytes. When the hostname exceeds that limit, Lease creation is rejected forever. Since v1.35, shutdown waits on that retry loop, causing a deadlock.

The retry loop logs:

```
    E0705 16:05:59 controller.go:201] "Failed to ensure lease exists, will retry"
    err="Lease.coordination.k8s.io \"apiserver-...\" is invalid: metadata.labels:
    Invalid value: \"sat12-dp146-...-FE94C5DD19A3.local\":
    must be no more than 63 bytes" interval="7s"
```
A goroutine dump after `SIGTERM` shows the shutdown hook blocked in `Stop()` while the lease controller is still retrying:

```
    goroutine 1 [sync.Mutex.Lock]:
    k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease.(*controller).Stop(...)
            k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller.go:131
    k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/controlplane/apiserver.completedConfig.New.func10()
            k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/controlplane/apiserver/server.go:279
    k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server.(*GenericAPIServer).RunPreShutdownHooks(...)

    goroutine 3459 [select]:
    k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease.(*controller).backoffEnsureLease(...)
            k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller.go:203
    k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease.(*controller).sync(...)
            k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller.go:174
```

The deadlock is:

1. `sync()` holds `reconcilingLock` and calls `backoffEnsureLease(ctx)`.
2. `backoffEnsureLease(ctx)` retries forever because the Lease can never be created.
3. On `SIGTERM`, the pre-shutdown hook calls `controller.Stop()`.
4. `Stop()` blocks waiting for `reconcilingLock`.
5. The retry context is only canceled after pre-shutdown hooks return.
6. Pre-shutdown hooks cannot return because `Stop()` is blocked.

This is not specific to hostnames. Any permanent `ensureLease` failure can block shutdown the same way.

This appears to have been introduced by #134514, shipped in v1.35.0. It is present in v1.35.x and v1.36.x, and not present in v1.34.x.

Fix: #140241. With that fix applied, the same setup exits about 2 seconds after `SIGTERM`.

### What did you expect to happen?

`SIGTERM` should shut down `kube-apiserver` within seconds.

If the identity Lease cannot be created, the identity feature should be degraded, but apiserver shutdown should not be blocked.

### How can we reproduce it?

Option A: component-level test

Run the regression test from #140241:

```
    TestStopDoesNotBlockWhenLeaseCannotBeCreated
```

in:

```
    staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller_test.go
```
Without the `controller.go` fix from that PR, `Stop()` never returns and the test times out after 30 seconds. With the fix, it passes quickly.

Option B: real binaries in containers

Adjust `arm64`/`amd64` as needed.

```
    mkdir repro && cd repro

    curl -sLo kube-apiserver https://dl.k8s.io/v1.36.2/bin/linux/arm64/kube-apiserver
    chmod +x kube-apiserver

    curl -sL https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/releases/download/v3.6.4/etcd-v3.6.4-linux-arm64.tar.gz \
      | tar xz --strip-components=1 etcd-v3.6.4-linux-arm64/etcd

    openssl genrsa -out sa.key 2048
    openssl rsa -in sa.key -pubout -out sa.pub

    cat > test.sh << 'EOF'
    #!/bin/bash

    /repro/etcd \
      --data-dir=/tmp/etcd \
      --listen-client-urls=http://127.0.0.1:2379 \
      --advertise-client-urls=http://127.0.0.1:2379 \
      >/tmp/etcd.log 2>&1 &

    sleep 3

    /repro/kube-apiserver \
      --etcd-servers=http://127.0.0.1:2379 \
      --cert-dir=/tmp/certs \
      --secure-port=6443 \
      --bind-address=127.0.0.1 \
      --advertise-address=$(hostname -i) \
      --authorization-mode=RBAC \
      --disable-admission-plugins=ServiceAccount \
      --service-cluster-ip-range=10.0.0.0/24 \
      --allow-privileged=true \
      --service-account-issuer=https://127.0.0.1:6443/ \
      --service-account-key-file=/repro/sa.pub \
      --service-account-signing-key-file=/repro/sa.key \
      >/tmp/apiserver.log 2>&1 &

    PID=$!

    sleep 20

    echo "lease errors: $(grep -c 'Failed to ensure lease exists' /tmp/apiserver.log)"

    kill -TERM $PID

    for i in $(seq 45); do
      kill -0 $PID 2>/dev/null || {
        echo "RESULT: exited ${i}s after SIGTERM"
        exit 0
      }
      sleep 1
    done

    echo "RESULT: STILL RUNNING 45s after SIGTERM"
    EOF
```

```
    docker run --rm --hostname "$(python3 -c "print('a'*61+'.lo')")" \
      -v "$PWD":/repro ubuntu:24.04 bash /repro/test.sh
```

Expected result with a 64-byte hostname:

```
    RESULT: STILL RUNNING 45s after SIGTERM
```

For comparison, a 63-byte hostname exits normally:

```
    docker run --rm --hostname "$(python3 -c "print('a'*60+'.lo')")" \
      -v "$PWD":/repro ubuntu:24.04 bash /repro/test.sh
```

Expected result:

    RESULT: exited 2s after SIGTERM

### Anything else we need to know?

This was found in Kubebuilder CI, which runs controller tests against real `kube-apiserver` and `etcd` binaries through controller-runtime envtest. Teardown sends `SIGTERM` and later `SIGKILL`; there is no kubelet or container runtime involved.

Public examples:

- macOS runner with a 68-byte hostname:
  https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kubebuilder/actions/runs/28746565395/job/85238353306?pr=5836
- Ubuntu runner with hostname set to 64 bytes:
  https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kubebuilder/actions/runs/28747687942/job/85241306371?pr=5836

This does not appear to be connection draining. There are no in-flight or watch requests, and no shutdown activity begins.

It also does not appear to be signal delivery. `etcd`, started the same way on the same host, exits in under a second on `SIGTERM`, and the hung apiserver handles `SIGQUIT` normally.

Full goroutine dumps and `-v=4` logs are available if helpful.

### Kubernetes version

Reproduced with official v1.35.0 and v1.36.2 release binaries.

Introduced in v1.35.0 by #134514.
Present in v1.35.x and v1.36.x.
Not present in v1.34.x.

### Cloud provider

None. Plain host processes on GitHub Actions runners and a laptop.

### OS version

Reproduced on macOS 15 arm64 and Ubuntu 24.04 amd64/arm64.

The deciding variable is hostname length, not OS. Linux caps hostnames at 64 bytes, so only a 64-byte hostname exceeds the 63-byte label value limit.

### Install tools

140300.title: KEP-5491: `matchAttribute` constraint fails to allocate devices when backtracking is required (DRAListTypeAttributes)
140300.body:
/wg device-management
/sig scheduling
KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5491

_This bug is originally reported by @pohly in a private communication._

### What happened?

When using `DRAListTypeAttributes` is enabled (list-type device attributes),  `matchAttribute` fails the device allcation even when a valid combination of devices exists.

For example, given four devices where attributes are lists of values:
- `dev1: attr=[1,2]`
- `dev2: attr=[1]`
- `dev3: attr=[2]`
- `dev4: attr=[2]`

The device allocator fails to find the valid allocation  `{dev1, dev3, dev4}`  because after removing  `dev2` during backtracking,  the intersection kept in the allocator is still  `{1}`  (stale from when  `dev2`  was added), causing  `dev3`  and  `dev4`  to be incorrectly rejected as below:

1. Add  `dev1`  → intersection becomes  `{1,2}` 
1. Add  `dev2`  → intersection shrinks to  `{1}` 
1. Try  `dev3`  →  `{2} ∩ {1} = ∅`  → rejected
1. Try  `dev4`  → same rejection
1. Backtrack: remove  `dev2`  →  only`numDevices`  goes to 1, but intersection is still  `{1}` (BUG) 
1. Retry  `dev3`  → rejected (wrong!  `{1,2} ∩ {2} = {2}`  is valid)
1. Allocation fails despite  `{dev1, dev3, dev4}`  being a valid solution

### What did you expect to happen?

The allocator should successfully return a valid set of 3 devices that satisfies the  `matchAttribute` constraint, such as  `{dev1, dev3, dev4}`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Enable the `DRAListTypeAttributes`  feature gate
2. Create devices with list-type attributes as described above (4 devices,  `attr` attribute as a list)
3. Create a  `ResourceClaim` requesting 3 devices with a `matchAttribute`  constraint on  `attr`
4. Observe that allocation fails despite `{dev1, dev3, dev4}` being a valid solution

### Anything else we need to know?

### Root cause (allocator internals):

The bug is in [`matchAttributeConstraint`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.2/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go#L865-L878) in [the experimental allocator](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.2/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go).

The allocator uses recursive depth-first search with backtracking. When a device is tentatively added to the `matchAttributeConstarint`, [`add()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.2/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go#L880) narrows the intersection to the running intersection of all device attribute sets. However, when the allocator backtracks and calls [`remove()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.2/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go#L965), the intersection is _never_ restored. Subsequent candidates are then evaluated against a stale, over-restricted intersection and incorrectly rejected.

Note: _`distinctAttributeConstraint` does not have this bug_ — it stores per-device attributes in a [`map[requestName]attribute` and correctly removes entries on backtrack](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/constraint.go#L41).

### Proposed fix approaches:

#### Option A: Intersection stack

Push the intersection before narrowing in `add()`, pop it back in `remove()`.

- ✅ `O(1)` per add/remove
- ⚠️ Relies on the allocator's device search order (it works today due to Depth-First search structure in the allocator, but is fragile to future refactors)

#### Option B: Store per-device sets, recompute on remove

Keep a `map[deviceID]deviceAttributeSet`; recompute the intersection from scratch in `remove()`. It is a similar approach to the `distinctAttributeConstraint` implementation

- ✅ Correct regardless of removal order
- ✅ Consistent with existing patterns in the codebase
- ⚠️ `O(n)` per remove — impact could be limited in practice since the number of search target devices would typically be single digits

Generally, _Option A_ would be preferred. I'd be glad to have feedback!

140436.title: DRA structured allocator leaks reserved counters and constraints when it rejects or backtracks a candidate device
140436.body:
### What happened?

The structured DRA allocator can leave reserved state behind when it stops considering a candidate device, which can make a schedulable pod fail to schedule.

`allocateDevice` reserves a device's shared counters and adds claim constraints before it may reject the candidate on a device taint or a claim constraint. For a candidate it accepts, it also reserves consumable capacity, and the backtracking search later has to undo all of that. Some of these paths did not reverse what they had done:

- A candidate rejected on a device taint or a claim constraint kept its reserved shared counters.
- The success undo for an allow-multiple device released its capacity but not the counters it had reserved on its first allocation, so backtracking leaked them.

A leaked counter reservation makes the allocator treat a counter set as exhausted, so it fails to allocate a device combination a node can satisfy, and a schedulable pod stays pending.

The consumable-capacity rejection path does not leak capacity, because the capacity check runs before the reservation. What it can leave behind is the claim constraint added just before the check.

### What did you expect to happen?

When the allocator rejects or backtracks a candidate, every reservation it made for that candidate (shared counters, claim constraints, device marking, consumable capacity) should be released, so a later candidate combination is evaluated against the correct available state.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Four cases in the shared `allocatortesting` table reproduce it. Each asserts the exact allocated devices:

- `partitionable-devices-taint-releases-counter`
- `partitionable-devices-constraint-releases-counter`
- `partitionable-consumable-capacity-backtrack-releases-counter`
- `consumable-capacity-rejection-rolls-back-constraints`

These cases are added by the fix PR, so to reproduce, apply only the `allocator_testing.go` test additions from #140431 onto the reported master commit, then run:

```console
cd staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation

go test \
  ./structured/internal/stable \
  ./structured/internal/incubating \
  ./structured/internal/experimental \
  -run 'TestAllocator/(partitionable-devices-taint-releases-counter|partitionable-devices-constraint-releases-counter|partitionable-consumable-capacity-backtrack-releases-counter|consumable-capacity-rejection-rolls-back-constraints)$' \
  -count=1
```

With only the regression-test changes applied, these cases fail on the reported master commit. They pass with the implementation changes from #140431.

The default feature configuration selects the incubating allocator (ConsumableCapacity and the device binding and status gates are on by default, and stable does not support them), so this is reachable on default clusters. The stable and experimental variants carry the same shape.

### Anything else we need to know?

Proposed fix: #140431.

That PR records what each `allocateDevice` call mutated in a `deviceRollbackState` value and reverses it with one `rollbackDevice` method, called on every rejection path after a counter reservation (including the `must` error path) and returned as the success undo, so the rejection cleanup and the backtracking undo can no longer drift apart. All three allocator variants are fixed together.

Two further cases in the same test table cover the fix rather than reproduce the master bug, so they pass on the reported master commit:

- `partitionable-empty-capacity-multiple-share-backtrack-keeps-counter-ownership`: for an allow-multiple device with no consumable capacity, its capacity-map entry doubles as the marker that lets a later share skip the counter check. The rollback must not delete it while another share is still active; doing so recharges the device's counter for a later share and rejects that share wrongly. This guards the new rollback against over-removing the marker.
- `partitionable-all-mode-constraint-must-error-with-reserved-counter`: exercises the `must` error path with a reserved counter. That error aborts the allocation, so the case locks the error contract and runs the rollback branch rather than reproducing a leak.

### Kubernetes version

```console
master at 16e45f3b5e6a76a1ac741550e3a65980eea783c2
Go 1.26
```

```text

DRAConsumableCapacity=true
```

Both are beta and enabled by default starting with Kubernetes 1.36.

### Cloud provider

```text
N/A - reproduced as a structured allocator unit test.
```

139914.title: Document caveats related to re-using the PodGroup name
139914.body:
### What happened?

/sig scheduling

A pod group may be recreated with the same names, for example:

* Delete Pod A
* Delete PodGroup B
* Create PodGroup B
* Create Pod A

These events may be observed by the scheduler in a different order:

* Delete Pod A
* Create Pod A
* Delete PodGroup B
* Add PodGroup B

If Pod A gets scheduled before PodGroup B is observed as re-created, it may break immutability assumptions, and cause unexpected scheduler behavior (both initially and in the following cycles).

### What did you expect to happen?

This problem arises from the fact that the PodGroup API uses resource names as parent links instead of UIDs, making it impossible to tell from the scheduler perspective whether the pod belongs to the old (deleted) PG or the new (created) PG if those PGs use the same name.

Since the scheduler handles pods with the same name but different UIDs fine, it could be understandable that users may assume the same for the higher-level hierarchies (PodGroups or CompositePodGroups). Because the actual behavior may be unexpected, it should be clearly described, and the recommendation to always assign new names to PodGroups (and CompositePodGroups) should be present somewhere, as otherwise there is no guarantee that the higher-level scheduling constraints will be respected by the scheduler.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Re-create the PG using the same names but with different PG field values. The order of events on the scheduler side is non-deterministic but can be:

1. Old pod is deleted
2. New pod is created
3. New pod is scheduled
4. Old pod group is deleted
5. New pod group is created, possibly with conflicting requirements with the newly scheduled pod

### What happened?

While looking at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/123545, I tried to validate the current behaviors about "healthz-bind-address" and "metrics-bind-address", and found some inconsistencies between the docs and the code.

1. According to the following usages, setting "--healthz-bind-address" and "--metrics-bind-address" to empty values should disable the two servers, however making such configurations doesn't really work. So it's either a doc issue or a code issue.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/54f9807e1e84981b2053f4daf779f5ed19962144/cmd/kube-proxy/app/server.go#L163-L164

2. Regardless of whether disabling the two servers should be supported or not, the validation code for the two addresses are inconsistent, it tolerates HealthzBindAddress to be empty but not MetricsBindAddress. kube-proxy wouldn't be up when MetricsBindAddress is empty.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/54f9807e1e84981b2053f4daf779f5ed19962144/pkg/proxy/apis/config/validation/validation.go#L73-L76

3. `HealthzServer` is only initialized when `HealthzBindAddress` is not empty. However, it's used by `NodeEligibleHandler` unconditionally, which would cause kube-proxy to panic when it's nil.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/54f9807e1e84981b2053f4daf779f5ed19962144/cmd/kube-proxy/app/server.go#L644-L646
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/54f9807e1e84981b2053f4daf779f5ed19962144/cmd/kube-proxy/app/server.go#L954-L956

It seems that regardless of whether we want to support disabling the two servers, some cleanup would be needed. But I'm not sure what's the expected behavior here.

Setting "--healthz-bind-address" and "--metrics-bind-address" to empty values, the two servers aren't disabled.
